mcq_picks.reasoning: The stimulus itself names the pre-revival condition: fewer colonists could testify to a conversion experience and church membership was shrinking. A is unsupported (no order from London is mentioned), B is false (Parliament did not ban dissenting churches in 1730), D contradicts the stimulus (the population was growing — children and grandchildren of the founders coming of age).

The petition is written by Easty herself from Salem jail, condemned to die, pleading that no more innocent blood be shed. It is the perspective of the accused facing execution. A names the accusers' testimony, which the petition does not contain; C and D name imperial policy and the judges' legal reasoning, neither of which the petition gives.

A jury acquitting against the Crown's prosecution is a check on royal authority. A is wrong (juries do not levy taxes), B is wrong (the trial was not about independence), D is wrong (the Navigation Acts were enforced by vice-admiralty courts, not juries).

An image published 1877-1896 is a 19th-century imagining, not a 1735 record, so it cannot show what the 1735 courtroom actually looked like. B is false (the jury acquitted Zenger, it did not find him guilty), C is false (the trial was in New York, not Philadelphia), D is false (the image proves nothing about what the judges thought during the trial).

The map names the Welch Tract, German Township, Radnor Township and Haverford Township — distinct groups settled in their own townships. A is contradicted by the Welsh and German names, B by the grid-plan inset of Philadelphia, C by the same Welsh/German names.

The table ties the labor force to the crop: tobacco, rice and indigo needed large plantation labor forces, while New England ran on fish, timber and small farms. A is not in the table (no population comparison supports it), B is false (slavery was legal in New England too — the table says a small share, not zero), D is false (the Chesapeake and Lower South were not settled by enslaved people).
